Chapter 8: The Market’s Limits—When Commerce Can’t Solve Everything
There's something comforting about believing the market can fix anything, isn't there? If a problem pops up, you just wait—someone will invent a product or service to solve it. And if something's really valuable, the market always finds a way to provide it.
But here's the thing: as we've seen, not everything that truly matters can be bought or sold.
Picture a family desperately searching for affordable housing in a city where prices aren't set by local needs, but by wealthy investors from across the globe. Or think about a community watching their once-public park become private property—suddenly, only those who can pay get to enjoy it.
Maybe you know a teacher struggling to explain to her students why the school can’t afford new books, even while the city around them gets richer.
Most of us don’t notice the market’s limits until we hit them head-on. It's easy to assume competition keeps things fair, and that more choices always lead to better outcomes.
But some things—like clean air, safe neighborhoods, or even just a sense of belonging—aren’t measured in dollars. When we start thinking the market is the only solution, these things get overlooked, or even lost.
It becomes obvious: the market is a powerful tool, but it makes a pretty lousy master. Sure, it can help create wealth, but it can’t create meaning. It can deliver all kinds of goods, but not justice.
The real glue that holds a society together—trust, solidarity, a sense of shared purpose—those aren’t things you can just pick up at a store.
All around us, you'll find examples of people stepping up to fill these gaps. Neighbors join forces to clean up a park, even when funding’s been slashed. Volunteers keep food banks, shelters, and clinics running—doing the work the market simply won’t.
And while these efforts are inspiring, they also shine a light on the limits of a system that puts profit above everything else.
So, what's the lesson here? It’s simple, but easy to forget: some things are just too important to leave up to the market.
The real challenge is remembering what those things are—and finding ways to protect them, even as the world keeps changing.
